parsed.explanation: The combined regime is dominated by national border and document exposure: passports and visas use sex assigned at birth, X markers are not processed, and a discrepancy can lead to secondary screening, refusal, confiscation or a material-misrepresentation/lifetime-ineligibility finding. National rules also restrict facilities congruent with gender identity, and federal custody has documented severe harm. The state/province layer is comparatively protective: anti-discrimination law covers public accommodations and health care, hate-crime enhancements exist, courts have enforced civil rights, and public support is high. But those protections do not bind national border officers, federal facilities or immigration custody. No general criminalisation of trans identity is documented; the main visitor exposure is denial/stranding plus federal facility exclusion, with lower-probability severe custody risk. This sits in the Elevated Risk band.

entry_documents.exposure: National rules require sex assigned at birth; X markers are not processed for new documents; discrepancies can trigger refusal, additional evidence demands, passport confiscation, or a material-misrepresentation/lifetime-ineligibility finding.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X passports remain valid until expiry; fraud findings are not automatic and require four elements; litigation and legal-aid guidance are available.
entry_documents.interaction: The traveller crosses national border screening before any state/province protection applies; state/province anti-discrimination law cannot bind national officers.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: National immigration custody has documented forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and sexual abuse; national corrections policies impose conversion-style practices on trans inmates.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Detention is not automatic; fraud findings require process; no state/province authority over federal custody is documented.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A border document discrepancy can escalate into national immigration detention, moving the traveller from a protective state/province into a hostile federal system.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National executive policy bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with gender identity; many states/provinces ban such access, and one documented bathroom arrest occurred under a state/province trespass law.
federal_state_facilities.protection: This state/province has public-accommodation protections covering gender identity since 2018/2020, and no state/province bathroom ban is documented for it.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: State/province protections cover many local venues but cannot cancel national facility rules or other states/provinces' bans.

care_services.exposure: This state/province bans gender-affirming medicine and surgery for minors; national proposals would restrict insurance coverage. No visitor-specific emergency-care denial is documented.
care_services.protection: State/province anti-discrimination law covers health care since 2020; adult care access is not documented as restricted for visitors.
care_services.interaction: A travelling minor may face state/province care restrictions if care is sought; an adult visitor's routine care access is not documented either way.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National counterterrorism rhetoric names 'radically pro-transgender' groups as a priority, and national executive orders frame gender ideology as a threat.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: This state/province has hate-crime enhancements since 2019 and documented civil-rights enforcement; a 2026 court found an attacker liable for striking a trans woman.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: National threat framing raises climate risk, but no state/province police targeting of trans visitors is documented.

minors_guardians.exposure: A trans minor's document mismatch at national border screening can expose them and their guardian to questioning; this state/province bans gender-affirming care for minors, and a sports ban is stayed.
minors_guardians.protection: State/province anti-bullying law covers gender identity, the high court protected trans students in 2024, and public-accommodation protections apply.
minors_guardians.interaction: A guardian cannot shield a minor from national border scrutiny; state/province care restrictions apply if care is sought.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: This state/province recorded 72 anti-LGBTQ incidents in 2025, the second-highest raw count, though no per-capita rate is published; one assault on a trans woman is documented.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Hate-crime penalty enhancements cover gender identity, anti-discrimination law is enforceable, and a court held an attacker liable in 2026; 88% poll support for protections.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: State/province courts and police provide a documented remedy for street violence, unlike the federal custody setting.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: National passport restrictions are litigated and their operative status may change; the fraud finding carries limited waiver; the incident census lacks a denominator; care-ban injunction status is unresolved.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Litigation, legal-aid FAQs, and state/province civil-rights enforcement provide partial recourse.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: The traveller must navigate variable national measures; state/province remedies do not reach national border or custody decisions.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.35-A involves an administrative delay resolved through an ombudsman and no detention. This case is worse because national border rules can refuse entry, confiscate documents, or trigger lifetime ineligibility, and federal facilities are restricted, though state/province protections are stronger.

0.45-A involves denial of boarding, a retained manifest, and open future consequences without detention. This case is similar in denial/stranding exposure but adds national passport confiscation, possible permanent fraud ineligibility, and federal facility exclusion, partly offset by robust state/province anti-discrimination enforcement.

0.65-A has a formal transit protection that works after public scrutiny. This case is materially lower because the decisive exposures are national border and facility rules that state/province protections cannot override; the visitor has no equivalent enforceable national protection.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime splits sharply by sovereign layer. State/province law is protective in accommodations, health care, hate crimes and civil-rights enforcement, and courts have acted for a trans victim. But the visitor first passes through national border screening where sex-assigned-at-birth rules, X-marker non-processing and discrepancy questioning can produce refusal, confiscation or a lifetime-ineligibility finding. National facility exclusion and severe federal custody conditions add lower-probability but high-severity exposure. No general criminalisation of trans identity is documented, so the result is not severe-risk; the combined effect is an Elevated Risk destination where state/province protections improve daily life but do not neutralise national border and federal-facility exposure.
